Partisanship in Belgian parliamentary speech, 1831–2025

From “Partisanship in Belgian Parliamentary Speech: Evidence from the Chamber of Representatives, 1831–2025”

These figures measure how distinctive the language of political groups is. Differences can come from the topics debated, the words chosen and the members who speak. A positive score means that a phrase tells more about a speaker’s group than the random-label benchmark does.

Reading the charts. A net value of +0.50 percentage points means that the classification score of a two-word phrase is 0.50 points above its shuffled-label benchmark. The bands labelled “80%” show the variation across subsamples of speakers.

03 / Topics and words

What makes language distinctive?

Explore the phrases behind the results and how much of the debate concerns each topic.

Which phrases distinguish political groups?

These two-word phrases contribute strongly to the estimated difference between the selected groups. The bars show how often each group uses them per 100,000 phrases. Common words are removed and words are stemmed, so the phrases may look incomplete (“chemin fer” represents “chemin de fer”). Procedural language, routine expressions, amounts and dates, personal names, and names of parties or parliamentary groups are excluded. A law with its year and an age can remain, as in “67 ans”.

Divide
Language

Linguistic differences within topics

Each speech is assigned to one of 24 topics, grouped into nine policy areas. A language model (gpt-6-luna) labelled a sample of passages, and two classifiers trained on these labels, CamemBERT for French and RobBERT for Dutch, classified all 3.1 million passages. On passages held out from training, they give the language model’s label in 74% of cases. A speech can touch several topics and is counted under its main one. Each chart compares wording within a topic. Values are net of the random-label benchmark, and the grey series is all speech.

04 / Parliamentary behaviour

Speech, voting and regional divisions

Contrast linguistic distinctiveness with observed votes and electoral geography.

Speech and voting disagreement

Do groups that speak more differently also vote more differently? Here linguistic partisanship is set beside the division in roll-call votes, measured as between-group voting distance. For each roll call, this is the absolute difference between the two groups’ shares of yes votes among the votes cast for and against, from 0 (identical shares) to 1 (unanimously opposed), averaged over the roll calls of the period. The correlations describe how the two measures move together. Periods with fewer than 20 roll calls, or with low coverage of the sittings, are left out.

Divide

Pairs of parties, since 1979

Each point is a pair of parties speaking the same language in one period: the division between the two parties in roll calls and the difference in their speech, as in “Party by party”. Parties in the same coalition usually vote alike, so the pairs on the same side, both in government or both in opposition for most of the period, are shown separately.

Flemish and Walloon members of the same party

Flemish and Walloon members

Regional comparability. “Flanders” and “Wallonia” are the electoral districts of the two regions. Brussels and, where indicated, Brussels–Halle–Vilvoorde are excluded. Flanders elects more members, so a positive Flemish balance of government seats is partly expected. The hover information gives the balance among all seats for comparison.

06 / Documentation

How to read the evidence

Definitions, uncertainty, coverage, limitations, sources and citation.

Methods, limitations and data

Partisanship

The measure follows Gentzkow, Shapiro and Taddy (2019, Econometrica). Each speech is linked to its speaker and party, cleaned and split into two-word phrases, after stemming and removing common words. Phrases without political content are left out: procedural formulas, courtesies and titles, names of people, parties and groups, amounts and dates. A law with its year and an age can remain, as in “67 ans”. For each period, a penalized statistical model estimates how often each group uses each phrase. The estimates for the main divides adjust for gender and province. From them we compute how well a single phrase identifies a speaker’s political group, where 50% is chance. We estimate the same model after shuffling the group labels at random, which gives a benchmark for chance and estimation noise, and subtract it. Shaded bands show the middle 80% of the estimates from random subsamples with one fifth of the speakers of each period. These subsampling ranges show how much an estimate moves with the speakers included. A change across periods needs the uncertainty of the difference between periods, which the ranges of single periods do not give.

How to interpret the results. A net estimate of +0.50 percentage points means that the model’s classification score exceeds the random-label benchmark by half a percentage point. It measures how distinctive the wording is. Levels and trends can reflect shifts in topic, language, individual speakers, party membership, OCR coverage or the conventions of parliamentary reporting. Pairwise comparisons are symmetric, so they cannot say which party changed direction. Comparisons over time describe the series as they are, with all these compositional changes included.

Limits of inference. Most intervals in the descriptive panels are speaker-subsampling ranges. Some differences in the question box combine the ranges of single periods as if they were independent, although the same speakers appear in several periods. Many party pairs and events are compared, and the 80% intervals are not adjusted for multiple testing. The event-study section reports which results keep a false discovery rate below 10%.

  • Periods group parliamentary sessions (usually around two years). Shaded columns mark limited coverage of sittings in 1832–1843 and 1992–1995. Apparent changes in these years may partly reflect missing records.
  • French and Dutch phrases are analysed separately and combined for the main historical divides. For comparisons between modern parties, Dutch and French are shown separately.
  • Left–right compares socialists and communists with liberals, N-VA and the radical right. Right–others compares the latter with all other parties. Flemish–Walloon compares members of the same parties, in French only, so it ends when the national parties split along language lines (1968–1978). Women–men compares women and men of the same party family.
  • Vertical lines mark plural voting (1894), proportional representation (1900), equal male suffrage (1919), women's suffrage (1949), the split of the national parties (1968–1978) and the federal Chamber (1995).
  • Minimum speakers per side: 20 for the main divides, 15 for party-family and topic comparisons, 10 for individual party pairs, and 8 for the comparisons of today’s parties against the rest. Periods below these minimums are left blank.
  • For party pairs, the direct score is symmetric: A versus B equals B versus A. It cannot show which party moved.

Topics

A companion module assigns a topic to every speech. A language model (gpt-6-luna) first labels agenda items from a sample of sittings, together with the subject keywords of the legislative files. These labels are grouped into 23 topics and a residual category for procedure. The language model then labels samples of passages of up to 300 words with this codebook. Two classifiers trained on those labels, CamemBERT for French and RobBERT-2023 for Dutch, classify all 3.1 million passages of the corpus. On passages held out from training, they give the language model’s label in 74% of cases. Each speech takes the topic with the highest mean probability across its passages, so a speech that covers several topics is counted under its main one. The 24 categories are grouped into nine policy areas. Partisanship by topic is estimated by legislature within the speeches of each topic or area, with the same model and random-label benchmark as the main series. These estimates have no intervals, so single legislatures are only indicative.

Reactions and emotions

A second module reads the stage directions written by the stenographers: disorder (interruptions, noise, protests and uproar), approval and laughter, and the chair’s calls to order and censures. Rates are per 100,000 words spoken by members, the chair excluded, or per 100 sittings. The module also finds references by name from one member to another, links them to members and ministers, and records whether they cross party families or language communities, compared with the share expected if speakers and targets were paired at random. These measures need no language model and cover the whole period. For the investiture and State of the Union debates since 1961, they give intervention counts close to those of Peeters and Lefever (2026) in most debates and similar shares of references across the language border. The coding of emotions in the speeches (eight categories, such as anger and fear) and of the tone of references (no attack, civil attack, uncivil attack) is in preparation: a language model has labelled samples of passages, two human coders will check part of them, and a multilingual classifier will extend the labels to all speeches.

Roll-call votes

Roll-call votes are read from the same reports, which list the members voting yes, no or abstaining, and are linked to the member register. For each roll call, between-group voting distance is the absolute difference between the two groups’ shares of “yes” votes among the “yes” and “no” votes cast: |YesA/(YesA+NoA) − YesB/(YesB+NoB)|. Abstentions are excluded, and so are roll calls without enough votes for or against in both groups. Zero means identical yes shares, and one means unanimously opposed votes. The period measure averages this distance over the roll calls that qualify. Periods with fewer than 20 roll calls are excluded. The groups are those of the speech series: Catholics, the left, the right and the government against all others, the left against the right, pairs of parties since 1979, women and men of the same party, and, until the national parties split, members of the same party elected in Flemish and in Walloon districts. The paper reports the Catholic, left and government comparisons. The others follow the same rules.

Data

The dataset uses available official plenary reports of the Belgian Chamber of Representatives, 1831–2025: the Annales parlementaires and, from 1999, the integral reports (CRIV). Text is segmented into speeches and linked to speakers, parties and constituencies where identified. Coverage is incomplete in some historical periods, as noted above.

Cite

Graziani, Riccardo. 2026. “Partisanship in Belgian Parliamentary Speech: Evidence from the Chamber of Representatives, 1831–2025.” Working paper, KU Leuven.
